claim: Aging and the age-associated decline of the proteome is determined in part through neuronal control of evolutionarily conserved transcriptional effectors.
source: Aging and the age-associated decline of the proteome is determined in part through neuronal control of evolutionarily conserved transcriptional effectors, which safeguard homeostasis under fluctuating metabolic and stress conditions by regulating an expansive proteostatic network.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that synthesizes the conceptual framework of the study, drawing on established scientific understanding of aging mechanisms.

claim: Caenorhabditis elegans homeodomain-interacting protein kinase (HPK-1) acts as a key transcriptional effector to preserve neuronal integrity, function, and proteostasis during aging.
source: We have discovered the Caenorhabditis elegans homeodomain-interacting protein kinase (HPK-1) acts as a key transcriptional effector to preserve neuronal integrity, function, and proteostasis during aging.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Loss of hpk-1 results in drastic dysregulation in expression of neuronal genes, including genes associated with neuronal aging.
source: Loss of hpk-1 results in drastic dysregulation in expression of neuronal genes, including genes associated with neuronal aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data presented in Figure 4 showing differential gene expression in hpk-1 null mutants.

claim: During normal aging hpk-1 expression increases throughout the nervous system more broadly than any other kinase.
source: During normal aging hpk-1 expression increases throughout the nervous system more broadly than any other kinase.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset shown in Figure 2I, demonstrating hpk-1 is upregulated in more cell clusters than any other kinase.

claim: Within the aging nervous system, hpk-1 induction overlaps with key longevity transcription factors.
source: Within the aging nervous system, hpk-1 induction overlaps with key longevity transcription factors, which suggests that hpk-1 expression mitigates natural age-associated physiological decline.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis in Figure 2C-D showing co-expression patterns of hpk-1 with longevity-associated transcription factors during aging.

claim: Pan-neuronal overexpression of hpk-1 extends longevity.
source: Consistently, pan-neuronal overexpression of hpk-1 extends longevity, preserves proteostasis both within and outside of the nervous system, and improves stress resistance.
evidence: This is demonstrated by lifespan assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pan-neuronal overexpression of hpk-1 preserves proteostasis both within and outside of the nervous system.
source: Consistently, pan-neuronal overexpression of hpk-1 extends longevity, preserves proteostasis both within and outside of the nervous system, and improves stress resistance.
evidence: This is supported by polyglutamine aggregation assays in neurons (Figure 5A-E) and muscle (Figure 5F-J).

claim: Pan-neuronal overexpression of hpk-1 improves stress resistance.
source: Consistently, pan-neuronal overexpression of hpk-1 extends longevity, preserves proteostasis both within and outside of the nervous system, and improves stress resistance.
evidence: This is demonstrated by thermotolerance assays shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Neuronal HPK-1 improves proteostasis through kinase activity.
source: Neuronal HPK-1 improves proteostasis through kinase activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with kinase-dead mutants (K176A and D272N) shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-F, which fail to improve proteostasis.

claim: HPK-1 functions cell non-autonomously within serotonergic and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic neurons to improve proteostasis in distal tissues.
source: HPK-1 functions cell non-autonomously within serotonergic and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic neurons to improve proteostasis in distal tissues by specifically regulating distinct components of the proteostatic network.
evidence: This is supported by tissue-specific overexpression experiments shown in Figure 7A-D demonstrating improved muscle proteostasis when hpk-1 is expressed in serotonergic or GABAergic neurons.

claim: Increased serotonergic HPK-1 enhances the heat shock response and survival to acute stress.
source: Increased serotonergic HPK-1 enhances the heat shock response and survival to acute stress.
evidence: This is demonstrated by thermotolerance assays (Figure 8A) and hsp-16.2p::GFP reporter expression (Figure 6B-C) in animals with serotonergic hpk-1 overexpression.

claim: GABAergic HPK-1 induces basal autophagy and extends longevity, which requires mxl-2 (MLX), hlh-30 (TFEB), and daf-16 (FOXO).
source: In contrast, GABAergic HPK-1 induces basal autophagy and extends longevity, which requires mxl-2 (MLX), hlh-30 (TFEB), and daf-16 (FOXO).
evidence: This is supported by autophagy reporter assays (Figure 8G-H) and genetic epistasis experiments (Figure 8J, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) showing requirement for these transcription factors.

claim: The gradual decline of function within the proteome (proteostasis) is a characteristic of aging.
source: The gradual decline of function within the proteome (proteostasis) is a characteristic of aging, which precipitates the onset and progression of a growing number of age-associated diseases (Balch et al., 2008; Gidalevitz et al., 2006; Gidalevitz et al., 2010; Kikis et al., 2010; Morimoto, 2011; Sala et al., 2017; Taylor and Dillin, 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature establishing this concept.

claim: Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are neurodegenerative diseases driven by genetic alterations that typically predispose a mutant protein isoform to aggregate and have toxic gain of function properties on the neuronal proteome.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are neurodegenerative diseases driven by genetic alterations that typically predispose a mutant protein isoform to aggregate and have toxic gain of function properties on the neuronal proteome.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: Age-associated proteostatic decline leads to diabetes mellitus outside of the nervous system.
source: Outside of the nervous system, age-associated proteostatic decline also leads to disease, for example, the onset of diabetes mellitus (Jaisson and Gillery, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The decline in proteostasis during normal aging is not limited to the nervous system.
source: Outside of the nervous system, age-associated proteostatic decline also leads to disease, for example, the onset of diabetes mellitus (Jaisson and Gillery, 2014); thus, the decline in proteostasis during normal aging is not limited to the nervous system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the example of diabetes mellitus and supported by citation.

claim: Aging is not simply the result of stochastic accumulation of damage, but is determined through genetics and coordinated mechanisms across tissues and cell types.
source: A growing number of studies suggest that aging is not simply the result of stochastic accumulation of damage, but is determined through genetics and coordinated mechanisms across tissues and cell types (Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015; Lazaro-Pena et al., 2022; López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Proteostatic decline corresponds with the age-associated breakdown of a large proteostasis network (PN), which integrates stress-responsive control of protein folding, degradation, and translation.
source: Proteostatic decline corresponds with the age-associated breakdown of a large proteostasis network (PN), which integrates stress-responsive control of protein folding, degradation, and translation in response to myriad cell intrinsic and non-autonomous signals.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding about the proteostasis network.

claim: How multi-cellular organisms maintain systemic proteostasis within and across tissues to delay aging is still poorly understood.
source: And yet, while major components of the proteostatic network have been identified, how multi-cellular organisms maintain systemic proteostasis within and across tissues to delay aging is still poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge, identifying a gap in understanding.

claim: Caenorhabditis elegans is a premier model system to elucidate how proteostasis is coordinated across cell and tissue types in response to myriad signals.
source: The relatively simple metazoan animal Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) is a premier model system to elucidate how proteostasis is coordinated across cell and tissue types in response to myriad signals.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of C. elegans as a model organism, based on established scientific consensus.

claim: Discoveries of cell non-autonomous signaling first made in C. elegans have evolutionarily conserved components.
source: Discoveries of cell non-autonomous signaling first made in C. elegans have evolutionarily conserved components, and revealed that the nervous system acts as a key cell non-autonomous regulator of organismal proteostasis and longevity (reviewed in Miller et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The nervous system acts as a key cell non-autonomous regulator of organismal proteostasis and longevity.
source: Discoveries of cell non-autonomous signaling first made in C. elegans have evolutionarily conserved components, and revealed that the nervous system acts as a key cell non-autonomous regulator of organismal proteostasis and longevity (reviewed in Miller et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: A pair of thermosensory neurons systemically regulate the heat shock response (HSR) in a serotonin-dependent manner.
source: For example, a pair of thermosensory neurons systemically regulate the heat shock response (HSR) in a serotonin-dependent manner (Prahlad et al., 2008; Tatum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A regulatory component from the GABAergic and cholinergic systems normally limits muscle cell proteostasis.
source: In contrast, a second regulatory component from the GABAergic and cholinergic systems normally limits muscle cell proteostasis (Garcia et al., 2007; Silva et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The first discovery of a putative link between HPK-1 and longevity was from a genome-wide RNAi screen that identified 103 genes essential for decreased insulin-like signaling (ILS) to extend longevity.
source: The first discovery of a putative link between the transcriptional cofactor homeodomain-interacting protein kinase (HPK-1) and longevity was from our genome-wide RNAi screen that identified 103 genes essential for decreased insulin-like signaling (ILS) to extend longevity (Samuelson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: In C. elegans, hpk-1 preserves proteostasis, stress response, and organismal longevity.
source: In C. elegans, hpk-1 preserves proteostasis, stress response, and organismal longevity (Berber et al., 2016; Das et al., 2017; Samuelson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: HPK-1 extends longevity through distinct genetic pathways defined by HSF-1 and the target of rapamycin complex 1 (TORC1).
source: Additionally, we have previously shown that HPK-1 extends longevity through distinct genetic pathways defined by HSF-1 and the target of rapamycin complex 1 (TORC1) (Das et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: Activation of HIPK family members by either metabolic or genotoxic stressors has been observed from yeast to mammals.
source: Activation by either metabolic or genotoxic stressors has been observed from yeast to mammals, suggesting that this family of transcriptional cofactors arose early in evolution to couple metabolic and stress signaling (Hofmann et al., 2003; Kim et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2008; Shojima et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and represents an inference about evolutionary conservation.

claim: Mammalian HIPK family members regulate the activity of transcription factors (TFs), chromatin modifiers, signaling molecules, and scaffolding proteins in response to cellular stress.
source: In general, mammalian HIPK family members regulate the activity of transcription factors (TFs), chromatin modifiers, signaling molecules, and scaffolding proteins in response to cellular stress (Calzado et al., 2007; de la Vega et al., 2012; Song and Lee, 2003a; Song and Lee, 2003b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Nutrient stress, such as glucose deprivation, can activate Hipk1 and Hipk2.
source: For example, nutrient stress, such as glucose deprivation, can activate Hipk1 and Hipk2 (Ecsedy et al., 2003; Garufi et al., 2013; Song and Lee, 2003b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Hyperglycemia triggers HIPK2 degradation via the proteasome.
source: Conversely, hyperglycemia triggers HIPK2 degradation via the proteasome (Baldari et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: HPK-1 functions as a key regulator of the proteostatic response, originating in the nervous system of C. elegans.
source: We have discovered that HPK-1 functions as a key regulator of the proteostatic response, originating in the nervous system of C. elegans.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: hpk-1 is the most broadly upregulated kinase during normal C. elegans aging, predominantly within the nervous system.
source: We find that hpk-1 is the most broadly upregulated kinase during normal C. elegans aging, predominantly within the nervous system, and acts to preserve neuronal function and proteostasis within the nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset shown in Figure 2I.

claim: hpk-1 acts to preserve neuronal function and proteostasis within the nervous system.
source: We find that hpk-1 is the most broadly upregulated kinase during normal C. elegans aging, predominantly within the nervous system, and acts to preserve neuronal function and proteostasis within the nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by neurodegeneration assays (Figure 3A-D), synaptic transmission assays (Figure 3E-F), and polyglutamine aggregation assays (Figure 5A-E).

claim: HPK-1 kinase activity within the nervous system initiates cell non-autonomous signals that trigger protective peripheral responses to maintain organismal homeostasis.
source: Further, HPK-1 kinase activity within the nervous system initiates cell non-autonomous signals that trigger protective peripheral responses to maintain organismal homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing neuronal hpk-1 overexpression improves muscle proteostasis (Figure 5F-J) and requires neurotransmission (Figure 5K-L, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: Serotonergic HPK-1 activity increases thermotolerance and protects the proteome from acute stress by enhancing the HSR, without increasing lifespan or altering basal autophagy.
source: Responses can qualitatively differ depending on the neuronal type from which they arise: serotonergic HPK-1 activity increases thermotolerance and protects the proteome from acute stress by enhancing the HSR, without increasing lifespan or altering basal autophagy.
evidence: This is supported by thermotolerance assays (Figure 8A), lifespan assays (Figure 8B), autophagy reporter assays (Figure 8C-D), and HSR reporter assays (Figure 6B-C).

claim: GABAergic HPK-1 activity induces autophagy and extends longevity, without altering thermotolerance.
source: In contrast, GABAergic HPK-1 activity induces autophagy and extends longevity, without altering thermotolerance.
evidence: This is supported by autophagy reporter assays (Figure 8G-H), lifespan assays (Figure 8F), and thermotolerance assays (Figure 8E).

claim: HPK-1 overexpression is sufficient to induce autophagy gene expression.
source: HPK-1 overexpression is sufficient to induce autophagy gene expression, and autophagosome formation requires hlh-30 (TFEB), mxl-2 (MLX), and daf-16 (FOXO) TFs.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 6L) showing increased expression of atg-18 and bec-1.

claim: Autophagosome formation induced by HPK-1 overexpression requires hlh-30 (TFEB), mxl-2 (MLX), and daf-16 (FOXO) TFs.
source: HPK-1 overexpression is sufficient to induce autophagy gene expression, and autophagosome formation requires hlh-30 (TFEB), mxl-2 (MLX), and daf-16 (FOXO) TFs.
evidence: This is supported by genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 8J and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Serotonergic HPK-1 signaling responds to acute proteotoxic stress.
source: We posit that serotonergic HPK-1 signaling responds to acute proteotoxic stress, whereas GABAergic HPK-1 responds to chronic metabolic changes mediated through TORC1 (Das et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings and prior work.

claim: GABAergic HPK-1 responds to chronic metabolic changes mediated through TORC1.
source: We posit that serotonergic HPK-1 signaling responds to acute proteotoxic stress, whereas GABAergic HPK-1 responds to chronic metabolic changes mediated through TORC1 (Das et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings and prior work.

claim: Each of the distinct adaptive responses from serotonergic and GABAergic neurons is sufficient to activate the PN and improve proteostasis outside of the nervous system.
source: Yet, each of these distinct adaptive responses is sufficient to activate the PN and improve proteostasis outside of the nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing both serotonergic and GABAergic hpk-1 overexpression improve muscle proteostasis (Figure 7A-D).

claim: Increased neuronal expression of hpk-1 was sufficient to increase lifespan by 17%.
source: Increased neuronal expression of hpk-1 was sufficient to increase lifespan by 17%, which is comparable to constitutive overexpression of hpk-1 throughout the soma (Figure 1A; Das et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Transgenic animals overexpressing hpk-1 in either muscular, intestinal, or hypodermal cells had no significant change in lifespan.
source: In contrast, transgenic animals overexpressing hpk-1 in either muscular, intestinal, or hypodermal cells had no significant change in lifespan (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: hpk-1 is broadly expressed during embryogenesis and larval development, but HPK-1 protein is only expressed within the nervous system in adult animals.
source: hpk-1 is broadly expressed during embryogenesis and larval development, but HPK-1 protein is only expressed within the nervous system in adult animals (Berber et al., 2013; Berber et al., 2016; Das et al., 2017; Raich et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: hpk-1 and orthologs have roles in development, differentiation, and cell fate specification.
source: Furthermore, hpk-1 and orthologs are known to have roles in development, differentiation, and cell fate specification (Berber et al., 2013; Blaquiere and Verheyen, 2017; Calzado et al., 2007; Hattangadi et al., 2010; Rinaldo et al., 2007; Rinaldo et al., 2008; Steinmetz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: HPK-1 functions primarily within the nervous system in adult animals to regulate aging.
source: Therefore, we conclude that HPK-1 functions primarily within the nervous system in adult animals to regulate aging.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tissue-specific overexpression experiments and prior knowledge about hpk-1 expression patterns.

claim: Increased expression of hpk-1 in neurons was sufficient to partially mitigate the locomotion defect of hpk-1 null mutants in response to active stimuli.
source: Increased expression of hpk-1 in neurons was sufficient to partially mitigate the locomotion defect of hpk-1 null mutants in response to active stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by locomotion assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Restoring hpk-1 exclusively within the nervous system prevented the premature age-associated decline in movement of hpk-1 null mutant animals.
source: Next, we tested whether restoring hpk-1 exclusively within the nervous system would prevent the premature age-associated decline in movement of hpk-1 null mutant animals. Indeed, restoring hpk-1 neuronal expression rescued the premature age-associated decline in movement of hpk-1 null mutant animals (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by video analysis of movement over the lifespan (Video 1).

claim: HPK-1 activity within the nervous system is sufficient to improve healthspan.
source: Thus, HPK-1 activity within the nervous system is sufficient to improve healthspan.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the locomotion rescue experiments.

claim: Neuronal hpk-1 rescue was sufficient to restore a wild-type lifespan in hpk-1 null mutant animals.
source: Lastly, neuronal hpk-1 rescue was sufficient to restore a wild-type lifespan in hpk-1 null mutant animals (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Restoring hpk-1 expression solely within the nervous system was sufficient to rescue the reduced thermotolerance of hpk-1 null mutant animals.
source: Restoring hpk-1 expression solely within the nervous system was sufficient to rescue the reduced thermotolerance of hpk-1 null mutant animals (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by thermotolerance assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: hpk-1 primarily acts within the nervous system to regulate aging and stress resistance.
source: Collectively, these findings are consistent with the notion that hpk-1 primarily acts within the nervous system to regulate aging and stress resistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: hpk-1 mRNA expression increases in wild-type animals during normal aging between day 2 and 10 of adulthood.
source: hpk-1 mRNA expression increases in wild-type animals during normal aging between day 2 and 10 of adulthood (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Adult C. elegans are composed of 959 somatic cells, of which 302 are neuronal; all somatic cells are post-mitotic and arise from an invariant lineage.
source: Adult C. elegans are composed of 959 somatic cells, of which 302 are neuronal; all somatic cells are post-mitotic and arise from an invariant lineage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans anatomy.

claim: The C. elegans Aging Atlas analysis identified 211 unique 'cell clusters' within the aging soma.
source: A recent comprehensive single-cell analysis of age-associated changes in gene expression throughout C. elegans identified 211 unique 'cell clusters' within the aging soma: groups of cells within a lineage or tissue defined by gene expression profiles (Roux et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the C. elegans Aging Atlas study.

claim: The C. elegans Aging Atlas analysis identified 124 neuronal cell clusters and obtained age-associated changes in gene expression for 122.
source: The 'C. elegans Aging Atlas' analysis identified 124 neuronal cell clusters and obtained age-associated changes in gene expression for 122, with high concordance of overall gene expression between neuron clusters to a previous project, which mapped the complete gene expression profiles of the C. elegans nervous system in late larval animals (The CeNGEN project, Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the C. elegans Aging Atlas and CeNGEN studies.

claim: hpk-1 expression increases during aging within 48 cell clusters: broadly within the nervous system and in 11 non-neuronal cell clusters.
source: Using the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset, in which differentially expressed genes were identified within each cell cluster in old versus young animals, we find that hpk-1 expression increases during aging within 48 cell clusters: broadly within the nervous system and in 11 non-neuronal cell clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: With aging, neuronal expression of hpk-1 increased within interneurons, motor neurons, sensory neurons, and all neuronal subtypes (cholinergic, dopaminergic, GABAergic, serotonergic, and glutamatergic).
source: With aging, neuronal expression of hpk-1 increased within interneurons, motor neurons, sensory neurons, and all neuronal subtypes (cholinergic, dopaminergic, GABAergic, serotonergic, and glutamatergic).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset.

claim: No cell clusters were found in which hpk-1 is downregulated during normal aging.
source: We found no cell clusters in which hpk-1 is downregulated during normal aging.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset.

claim: Many longevity-associated TFs increase lifespan when overexpressed, and conversely hasten aging when lost.
source: It is well known that many longevity-associated TFs increase lifespan when overexpressed and shorten lifespan when lost (reviewed in Denzel et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Many longevity-associated TFs are upregulated during normal aging in more than 200 cell clusters.
source: A major finding of the C. elegans Aging Atlas study was that many longevity-associated TFs are upregulated during normal aging in more than 200 cell clusters (Roux et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the C. elegans Aging Atlas study.

claim: Increased expression of longevity-associated TFs is thought to reflect an age-associated adaptive response to dysregulation of homeostatic mechanisms and accumulating damage.
source: Increased expression of longevity-associated TFs is thought to reflect an age-associated adaptive response to dysregulation of homeostatic mechanisms and accumulating damage (Roux et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation to the C. elegans Aging Atlas study.

claim: Seventy-one TFs were differentially upregulated with hpk-1 during aging within 3 or more neuron clusters.
source: Seventy-one TFs were differentially upregulated with hpk-1 during aging within 3 or more neuron clusters, 30 within non-neuronal clusters, with an overlap of 21 TFs between neurons and non-neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: 26 of the TFs upregulated with hpk-1 during aging have previously been implicated in longevity.
source: Overall, 26 of these TFs have previously been implicated in longevity.
evidence: This is based on comparison with curated lists of longevity-associated genes.

claim: There are 10 TFs broadly upregulated with aging in the nervous system that overlap with hpk-1 (significant differential expression in 9 or more neuronal clusters).
source: There are 10 TFs broadly upregulated with aging in the nervous system that overlap with hpk-1 (significant differential expression in 9 or more neuronal clusters), 6 of which have previously been linked to longevity: daf-16 (FOXO, overlaps in 19/37 neuronal clusters), hlh-30 (TFEB, 18/37), dpy-22 (mediator complex subunit 12L, 15/37), gei-3 (10/37), skn-1 (NRF2, 10/37), and hif-1 (hypoxia inducible factor 1, 10/37) (Figure 2C; An and Blackwell, 2003; Chen et al., 2009; Fawcett et al., 2015; Kenyon et al., 1993; Lapierre et al., 2013; Lin et al., 1997; Ogg et al., 1997; Roux et al., 2022; Suriyalaksh et al., 2022; Tacutu et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset shown in Figure 2C and citations to prior studies.

claim: 12 TFs exhibited an inverse correspondence with hpk-1, and were largely downregulated with aging in the same neurons where hpk-1 is normally upregulated (significant differential expression in nine or more neuronal clusters).
source: Conversely, 12 TFs exhibited an inverse correspondence, and were largely downregulated with aging in the same neurons where hpk-1 is normally upregulated (significant differential expression in nine or more neuronal clusters) (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset shown in Figure 2D.

claim: xbp-1 (X-box binding protein 1) is a key regulator of the endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response (ER-UPR) and has been implicated in longevity.
source: only two of which have previously been implicated in longevity: xbp-1 (X-box binding protein 1) a key regulator of the endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response (ER-UPR), and mdl-1 (MAX dimerization protein) (Johnson et al., 2014; Nakamura et al., 2016; Riesen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: mdl-1 is a Myc-family member with opposing roles in longevity from mxl-2 (Mlx).
source: Of note, mdl-1 is a Myc-family member with opposing roles in longevity from mxl-2 (Mlx) (Johnson et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: mxl-2 is required for hpk-1 to extend longevity.
source: and mxl-2 is required for hpk-1 to extend longevity (Das et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: Both hpk-1 and gei-1 were significantly induced in older animals, and conversely xbp-1 expression was decreased.
source: As expected, both hpk-1 and gei-1 were significantly induced in older animals, and conversely xbp-1 expression was decreased (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: hpk-1 is significantly upregulated within isolated C. elegans neurons during normal aging.
source: As expected, we find that hpk-1 is significantly upregulated within isolated C. elegans neurons during normal aging (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Within neuronal cell clusters, hpk-1 and the longevity-associated TFs are broadly expressed throughout the nervous system by late larval development, with the exception of the nematode-specific gene gei-3.
source: Within neuronal cell clusters, hpk-1 and the aforementioned longevity-associated TFs are broadly expressed throughout the nervous system by late larval development, with the exception of the nematode-specific gene gei-3, for which overlap is restricted to a subset of neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: TFs with age-associated increases in expression in clusters overlapping with hpk-1 are associated with positive regulation of adult lifespan, heat and oxidative stress response, bacterial innate immunity, chromatin remodeling, development, mitophagy, axon regeneration, neddylation, and ubiquitination.
source: TFs with age-associated increases in expression in clusters overlapping with hpk-1 are associated with positive regulation of adult lifespan, heat and oxidative stress response, bacterial innate immunity, chromatin remodeling, development, mitophagy, axon regeneration, neddylation, and ubiquitination (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis of genes shown in Figure 2G.

claim: TFs with decreased expression in aging in hpk-1-upregulated neuronal cell clusters have been implicated in the ER unfolded protein response and the innate immune response.
source: TFs with decreased expression in aging in hpk-1-upregulated neuronal cell clusters have been implicated in the ER unfolded protein response and the innate immune response (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis of genes shown in Figure 2H.

claim: hpk-1 is upregulated in more cell clusters than any other kinase.
source: hpk-1 is upregulated in more cell clusters than any other kinase, while hpk-1 is upregulated in 48, the next most broadly upregulated kinase is gcy-28 (natriuretic peptide receptor 1, 38 cell clusters) (Li and van der Kooy, 2018; Shinkai et al., 2011; Tsunozaki et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset shown in Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: 115 kinases are upregulated and conversely 120 are downregulated in at least one cell cluster during aging, while 254 kinases do not change expression.
source: We were surprised to find that hpk-1 mRNA expression increased during aging, as kinase regulation at the level of gene expression seemed atypical. Therefore, using the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset we assessed whether any of the 438 C. elegans kinases (Zaru et al., 2017) are differentially expressed during aging: 115 kinases are upregulated and conversely 120 are downregulated in at least one cell cluster, while 254 kinases do not change expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Only 14 kinases are downregulated in 10 or more cell clusters during aging.
source: Only 14 kinases are downregulated in 10 or more cell clusters.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset.

claim: 20 kinases are upregulated in 10 or more cell clusters during aging.
source: Conversely, 20 kinases are upregulated in 10 or more cell clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: In addition to hpk-1 and gcy-28, five kinases previously linked to longevity are upregulated during aging: nipi-3, aak-1, scd-2, rsks-1, and smg-1.
source: In addition to hpk-1 and gcy-28, five kinases previously linked to longevity are upregulated: nipi-3 (a Tribbles pseudokinase that regulates SKN-1; Wu et al., 2021), aak-1 (AMP-activated kinase catalytic subunit alpha-2) (Lee et al., 2009), scd-2 (ALK receptor tyrosine kinase) (Shen et al., 2007), rsks-1 (ribosomal protein S6 kinase) (Hansen et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2007), and smg-1 (SMG1) (Masse et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset and citations to prior studies.

claim: HPK-1 is an essential component of TORC1-mediated longevity and autophagy.
source: We previously demonstrated that HPK-1 is an essential component of TORC1-mediated longevity and autophagy (Das et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: Only 2 of 11 TOR-associated genes, rsks-1 and aak-1, are upregulated during aging in three or more cell clusters.
source: Interestingly, we find that only 2 of 11 TOR-associated genes, rsks-1 and aak-1, are upregulated during aging in three or more cell clusters (Blackwell et al., 2019; Hindupur et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset and citations to prior studies.

claim: rsks-1 is exclusively upregulated outside of the nervous system and has poor overlap with hpk-1 (2/13).
source: We find rsks-1 is exclusively upregulated outside of the nervous system and has poor overlap with hpk-1 (2/13).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset.

claim: aak-1 is primarily but not exclusively upregulated outside of the nervous system during aging, with some overlap with hpk-1.
source: aak-1 is primarily but not exclusively upregulated outside of the nervous system during aging, with some overlap with hpk-1.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset.

claim: Aged populations of hpk-1 mutant animals displayed more than a threefold difference in VD axonal breaks and more than a twofold difference in DD axonal breaks compared to wild-type animals.
source: Aged populations of hpk-1 mutant animals displayed more than a threefold difference in VD axonal breaks and more than a twofold difference in DD axonal breaks compared to wild-type animals (Figure 3A–B and D).
evidence: This is supported by neurodegeneration assay data shown in Figure 3A-B and D.

claim: Young wild-type and hpk-1 mutant animals did not show neuronal breaks.
source: Importantly, young wild-type and hpk-1 mutant animals did not show neuronal breaks (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by neurodegeneration assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Loss of hpk-1 does not disrupt axon formation during development, rather HPK-1 preserves axonal integrity in aging motor neurons.
source: Thus, loss of hpk-1 does not disrupt axon formation during development, rather HPK-1 preserves axonal integrity in aging motor neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurodegeneration assay data.

claim: hpk-1 mutants showed increased aldicarb resistance by L4/YA.
source: Interestingly, hpk-1 mutants showed increased aldicarb resistance by L4/YA (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is supported by aldicarb paralysis assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Loss of hpk-1 reduces cholinergic synaptic transmission.
source: Interestingly, hpk-1 mutants showed increased aldicarb resistance by L4/YA (Figure 3E), suggesting that loss of hpk-1 reduces cholinergic synaptic transmission and that HPK-1 normally preserves neuronal function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the aldicarb resistance phenotype.

claim: Late L4/YA hpk-1 mutant animals paralyzed sooner in response to exogenous 5-HT: at 2 min of 5-HT treatment, 63% of mutants were immobilized compared to 25% of wild-type animals immobilized.
source: In a paralysis assay with exogenous 5-HT, we observed that late L4/YA hpk-1 mutant animals paralyzed sooner: at 2 min of 5-HT treatment, 63% of mutants were immobilized compared to 25% of wild-type animals immobilized (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by 5-HT paralysis assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: HPK-1 prevents an age-associated decline in axonal and synaptic integrity.
source: Based on the aforementioned findings, we conclude that HPK-1 prevents an age-associated decline in axonal and synaptic integrity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurodegeneration and synaptic transmission assays.

claim: Differential expression analysis identified 2201 total genes with significant expression changes with loss of hpk-1, 1853 upregulated and 348 downregulated.
source: Differential expression analysis identified 2201 total genes with significant expression changes with loss of hpk-1, 1853 upregulated and 348 downregulated (adjusted p-value <0.05 and log2 fold-change magnitude ≥1) (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Among downregulated genes in hpk-1 mutants, there are 25 genes implicated in the innate immune response, as well as TGF-beta and WNT signaling, glycosphingolipid metabolism, and surfactant metabolism.
source: Among downregulated genes, we find 25 genes implicated in the innate immune response, as well as TGF-beta and WNT signaling (five ubiquitin ligase complex component genes), glycosphingolipid metabolism, and surfactant metabolism (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The most significantly enriched single term among upregulated genes in hpk-1 mutants reveals a substantial number of cuticle and collagen-associated genes as dysregulated.
source: The most significantly enriched single term reveals a substantial number of cuticle and collagen-associated genes as dysregulated (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A striking number of functions significantly enriched in the hpk-1 upregulated genes are related to neuronal function and signaling, including neuropeptide and neurotransmitter pathways, mechanosensation, chemotaxis, and axon guidance.
source: A striking number of other functions significantly enriched in the hpk-1 upregulated genes from across GO, KEGG, and Reactome are related to neuronal function and signaling, including neuropeptide and neurotransmitter pathways, mechanosensation, chemotaxis, and axon guidance, among others (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Among 1496 genes known, or expected through homology, to function in the nervous system, 264 are upregulated with loss of hpk-1, representing a much larger overlap than expected by chance.
source: Among 1496 genes known, or expected through homology, to function in the nervous system, 264 are upregulated with loss of hpk-1, representing a much larger overlap than expected by chance (hypergeometric test p-value <0.0001) (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data in the context of curated gene lists.

claim: 15% of all hpk-1 upregulated genes are enriched or specific to neurons in wild-type animals (283 genes).
source: We found that 15% of all hpk-1 upregulated genes are enriched or specific to neurons in wild-type animals (283 genes, hypergeometric test p-value <0.0001)
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data in the context of tissue-specific gene expression data.

claim: Only five hpk-1 downregulated genes normally exhibit neuron-restricted expression.
source: whereas only five hpk-1 downregulated genes normally exhibit such neuron-restricted expression.
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data in the context of tissue-specific gene expression data.

claim: Functions over-represented among the upregulated neuronally expressed genes in hpk-1 mutants include neurotransmitter and ion transport, synaptic components and signaling, axon and neuron projection components, feeding and locomotion behavior, mechanosensation and touch-responsive behavior.
source: Representing these results as a network, and clustering terms which have overlapping gene associations, we identified some major themes: neurotransmitter and ion transport, synaptic components and signaling, axon and neuron projection components, feeding and locomotion behavior, mechanosensation and touch-responsive behavior are all upregulated in the absence of hpk-1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Among all genes upregulated in the hpk-1 null mutants, the largest group correspond to genes related to neuropeptide encoding, processing, and receptors.
source: Among all genes upregulated in the hpk-1 null mutants, the largest group correspond to genes related to neuropeptide encoding, processing, and receptors.
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Of the 120 neuropeptide-encoding genes in the C. elegans genome, 40 (33%) are upregulated in the hpk-1 null mutants.
source: Of the 120 neuropeptide-encoding genes in the C. elegans genome, 40 (33%) are upregulated in the hpk-1 null mutants.
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Nine insulin-related (ins) neuropeptide genes are upregulated in hpk-1 null mutants.
source: Nine of these are insulin-related (ins), which suggest increased hpk-1 expression during normal aging or hpk-1 overexpression may positively affect longevity through decreased ins neuropeptide expression.
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data and represents an inference about mechanism.

claim: Loss of hpk-1 upregulates expression of a number of neuronal genes including those involved in neuropeptide signaling, neurotransmission, release of synaptic vesicles, calcium homeostasis, and function of sensory neurons.
source: We conclude that loss of hpk-1 upregulates expression of a number of neuronal genes including those involved in neuropeptide signaling, neurotransmission, release of synaptic vesicles, calcium homeostasis, and function of sensory neurons (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Animals with pan-neuronal hpk-1 overexpression showed a decreased number of fluorescent foci within the nerve ring.
source: We measured polyglutamine toxic aggregate formation in neuronal cells (rgef-1p::Q40::YFP) of animals overexpressing hpk-1 pan-neuronally (rab-3p). These animals showed a decreased number of fluorescent foci within the nerve ring (Figure 5Ai–iii, B).
evidence: This is supported by polyglutamine aggregation assay data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Increased neuronal expression of hpk-1 significantly increased the average number of body bends (17.7±1 vs 12.5±1.2 bends/30 s).
source: Increased neuronal expression of hpk-1 significantly increased the average number of body bends (17.7±1 vs 12.5±1.2 bends/30 s), suggesting that neuronal expression of hpk-1 improves proteostasis in the nervous system and mitigates locomotion defects associated with the decline in proteostasis (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Animals with neuronal hpk-1 inactivation had a significant increase in foci number within neurons and a decreased number of body bends in liquid (19.7±0.8 vs 25.5±1.1 bends/30 s).
source: Animals with neuronal hpk-1 inactivation had a significant increase in foci number within neurons and a decreased number of body bends in liquid (19.7±0.8 vs 25.5±1.1 bends/30 s) (Figure 5Aiv, D, E).
evidence: This is supported by polyglutamine aggregation and locomotion assay data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: HPK-1 functions cell intrinsically to maintain neuronal proteostasis.
source: Thus, HPK-1 functions cell intrinsically to maintain neuronal proteostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neuronal RNAi experiments.

claim: Animals with increased neuronal hpk-1 expression had significantly decreased fluorescent foci in muscle tissue.
source: Animals with increased neuronal hpk-1 expression had significantly decreased fluorescent foci in muscle tissue (Figure 5Fi–ii). For instance, at day 3 of adulthood, animals overexpressing neuronal HPK-1 had an average of 21±0.9 polyQ aggregates, while control animals had an average of 26±1.1 polyQ aggregates (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by polyglutamine aggregation assay data in muscle shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: Increased hpk-1 expression in neurons was sufficient to reduce paralysis; at day 13 of adulthood only 61%±0.10 of neuronal hpk-1 overexpressing animals were paralyzed compared to 81%±0.08 of paralyzed control animals.
source: Of note, increased hpk-1 expression in neurons was sufficient to reduce paralysis; at day 13 of adulthood only 61%±0.10 of neuronal hpk-1 overexpressing animals were paralyzed compared to 81%±0.08 of paralyzed control animals (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by paralysis assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Increased neuronal HPK-1 activity is sufficient to improve proteostasis cell non-autonomously.
source: Thus, increased neuronal HPK-1 activity is sufficient to improve proteostasis cell non-autonomously.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the muscle proteostasis assays with neuronal hpk-1 overexpression.

claim: The kinase domain of HPK-1 is highly conserved from yeast to mammals, both at the amino acid level and predicted tertiary structure.
source: We find the kinase domain of HPK-1 is highly conserved from yeast to mammals, both at the amino acid level and predicted tertiary structure, based on multiple sequence alignments, AlphaFold structure prediction, and visualization with PyMol (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; DeLano, 2002; Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: K176A and D272N mutations are known to be essential for the kinase activity of HPK-1 orthologs.
source: We mutated two highly conserved residues within the kinase domain, K176A and D272N, which are known to be essential for the kinase activity of HPK-1 orthologs (He et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Kinase-dead mutant versions of HPK-1 (K176A and D272N) had no effect on either polyglutamine foci accumulation or paralysis in muscle cells when neuronally overexpressed.
source: In contrast to wild-type HPK-1 (Figure 5G and H), neither mutant had any effect on either polyglutamine foci accumulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D) or paralysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F) in muscle cells (unc-54p::Q35::YFP)
evidence: This is supported by polyglutamine aggregation and paralysis assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: Increased hpk-1 expression improves proteostasis through kinase activity.
source: thus, increased hpk-1 expression improves proteostasis through kinase activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinase-dead mutant experiments.

claim: Neuronal inactivation of hpk-1 was sufficient to hasten the collapse of proteostasis, significantly increasing the number of polyQ aggregates (45±1 vs 32±1.1 at day 4) and paralysis rate (84%±0.04 vs 14%±0.04 at day 9).
source: Neuronal inactivation of hpk-1 (sid-1(pk3321); unc-119p::sid-1; unc-54p::Q35::YFP; hpk-1(RNAi)) was sufficient to hasten the collapse of proteostasis, significantly increasing the number of polyQ aggregates (45±1 vs 32±1.1 at day 4) and paralysis rate (84%±0.04 vs 14%±0.04 at day 9) (Figure 5Fiii, I, J).
evidence: This is supported by polyglutamine aggregation and paralysis assay data shown in Figure 5I-J.

claim: HPK-1 function within the nervous system impacts proteostasis in distal muscle tissue.
source: Thus, HPK-1 function within the nervous system impacts proteostasis in distal muscle tissue, which implies that HPK-1 coordinates organismal health through cell non-autonomous mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neuronal RNAi experiments showing effects on muscle proteostasis.

claim: Neuronal expression of hpk-1 in unc-31 mutants improved proteostasis in the absence of neuropeptide transmission and dense core vesicles.
source: Neuronal expression of hpk-1 in unc-31 mutants improved proteostasis in the absence of neuropeptide transmission and dense core vesicles, as increased neuronal hpk-1 expression still delayed the age-associated accumulation of aggregates within muscle cells.
evidence: This is supported by polyglutamine aggregation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In the absence of neurotransmitter function, neuronal expression of hpk-1 in unc-13 mutants failed to improve proteostasis in muscle tissue.
source: In contrast, in the absence of neurotransmitter function, neuronal expression of hpk-1 in unc-13 mutants failed to improve proteostasis in muscle tissue (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by polyglutamine aggregation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: HPK-1-mediated longevity-promoting cell non-autonomous signaling occurs through neurotransmission.
source: We conclude that HPK-1-mediated longevity-promoting cell non-autonomous signaling occurs through neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the unc-31 and unc-13 mutant experiments.

claim: Increased neuronal expression of hpk-1 in wild-type animals did not alter the basal expression of molecular chaperones.
source: Increased neuronal expression of hpk-1 in wild-type animals did not alter the basal expression of molecular chaperones (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by hsp-16.2p::GFP reporter data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: After heat shock, increased neuronal hpk-1 expression resulted in hyper-induction of hsp-16.2p::GFP expression, particularly in the pharynx and head muscles, but not within intestinal cells.
source: In contrast, after heat shock, increased neuronal hpk-1 expression resulted in hyper-induction of hsp-16.2p::GFP expression, particularly in the pharynx and head muscles, but surprisingly not within intestinal cells (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: This is supported by hsp-16.2p::GFP reporter data after heat shock shown in Figure 6B-E.

claim: While hpk-1 is required for the broad induction of molecular chaperones, neuronal HPK-1 primes inducibility of the HSR within specific tissues, rather than in a systemic manner throughout the organism.
source: We conclude that while hpk-1 is required for the broad induction of molecular chaperones (Das et al., 2017), neuronal HPK-1 primes inducibility of the HSR within specific tissues, rather than in a systemic manner throughout the organism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HSR reporter experiments and prior work.

claim: Increased neuronal hpk-1 expression significantly induces autophagy in neurons and hypodermal seam cells, but not in the intestine.
source: Using two LGG-1/Atg8 fluorescent reporter strains to visualize autophagosome levels in neurons (rgef-1p::GFP::LGG-1), hypodermal seam cells, and intestine (lgg-1p::GFP::LGG-1) (Kumsta et al., 2017), we found that increased neuronal hpk-1 expression significantly induces autophagy in neurons and hypodermal seam cell (Figure 6F–I), but not in the intestine (Figure 6J and K).
evidence: This is supported by autophagy reporter assay data shown in Figure 6F-K.

claim: Increased neuronal overexpression of hpk-1 induces expression of atg-18 (WD repeat domain, phosphoinositide interacting 2) and bec-1 (Beclin 1).
source: We tested whether neuronal overexpression of hpk-1 is sufficient to induce autophagy gene expression, and found that increased neuronal overexpression induces expression of atg-18 (WD repeat domain, phosphoinositide interacting 2) and bec-1 (Beclin 1) (Figure 6L).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6L.

claim: Increased HPK-1 activity within the nervous system is sufficient to induce basal levels of autophagy both cell intrinsically and non-autonomously.
source: Thus, increased HPK-1 activity within the nervous system is sufficient to induce basal levels of autophagy both cell intrinsically and non-autonomously, which we posit occurs through increased autophagy gene expression to extend longevity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the autophagy reporter and gene expression experiments.

claim: Increased hpk-1 expression in glutamatergic or dopaminergic neurons was not sufficient to decrease the formation of fluorescent foci or reduce paralysis.
source: Increased hpk-1 expression in glutamatergic or dopaminergic neurons was not sufficient to decrease the formation of fluorescent foci or reduce paralysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by polyglutamine aggregation and paralysis assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increased expression of hpk-1 in either serotonergic (tph-1p::hpk-1) or GABAergic (unc-47p::hpk-1) neurons was sufficient to improve proteostasis in muscle tissue.
source: In contrast, increased expression of hpk-1 in either serotonergic (tph-1p::hpk-1) or GABAergic (unc-47p::hpk-1) neurons was sufficient to improve proteostasis in muscle tissue (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is supported by polyglutamine aggregation and paralysis assay data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: hpk-1 is expressed in serotonergic and GABAergic neurons.
source: Accordingly, we found that hpk-1 is expressed in serotonergic and GABAergic neurons, based on colocalization between hpk-1 and neuronal cell-type specific reporters (Figure 7E and F, Figure 7—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data showing colocalization in Figure 7E-F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increased HPK-1 serotonergic signaling was sufficient to improve thermotolerance, without altering lifespan or autophagy.
source: Increased HPK-1 serotonergic signaling was sufficient to improve thermotolerance, without altering lifespan or autophagy (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: This is supported by thermotolerance, lifespan, and autophagy assay data shown in Figure 8A-D.

claim: Increased hpk-1 expression in GABAergic neurons did not alter thermotolerance, but induced autophagy and slightly but significantly increased lifespan.
source: In contrast, increased hpk-1 expression in GABAergic neurons did not alter thermotolerance, but induced autophagy slightly but significantly increased lifespan (Figure 8E–H).
evidence: This is supported by thermotolerance, autophagy, and lifespan assay data shown in Figure 8E-H.

claim: Loss of tph-1 failed to block the induction of autophagy by increased neuronal hpk-1 expression.
source: As expected, loss of tph-1, which encodes the C. elegans tryptophan hydroxylase 1 essential for biosynthesis of serotonin (Sze et al., 2000), failed to block the induction of autophagy by increased neuronal hpk-1 expression (Figure 8I, tph-1(mg280);rab-3p::hpk-1).
evidence: This is supported by autophagy reporter assay data shown in Figure 8I.

claim: Loss of unc-30 was sufficient to completely abrogate the induction of autophagy in seam cells after increased pan-neuronal expression of hpk-1.
source: Consistent with our previous result demonstrating that only GABAergic expression of hpk-1 promotes autophagy, loss of unc-30 was sufficient to completely abrogate the induction of autophagy in seam cells after increased pan-neuronal expression of hpk-1 (Figure 8I, unc-30(ok613);rab-3p::hpk-1).
evidence: This is supported by autophagy reporter assay data shown in Figure 8I.

claim: HPK-1 activity in serotonergic neurons promotes systemic thermotolerance, whereas HPK-1 in GABAergic neurons promotes autophagy.
source: We conclude that HPK-1 activity in serotonergic neurons promotes systemic thermotolerance, whereas HPK-1 in GABAergic neurons promotes autophagy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell-type specific overexpression experiments.

claim: hpk-1 overexpression in GABAergic neurons still significantly induced autophagosomes in seam cells after loss of hsf-1 or pha-4.
source: Using feeding-based RNAi, we found that hpk-1 overexpression in GABAergic neurons still significantly induced autophagosomes in seam cells after loss of hsf-1 or pha-4 (Figure 8J)
evidence: This is supported by autophagy reporter assay data with RNAi shown in Figure 8J.

claim: HPK-1 induction of autophagy is independent of hsf-1 and pha-4.
source: thus HPK-1 induction of autophagy is independent of hsf-1 and pha-4 and suggests the pha-4 requirement for HPK-1-mediated longevity is independent of autophagy gene regulation (at least in hypodermal seam cells).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments.

claim: After inactivation of mxl-2, hlh-30, or daf-16, GABAergic overexpression of hpk-1 failed to significantly increase autophagosomes.
source: In contrast, after inactivation of mxl-2, hlh-30, or daf-16, GABAergic overexpression of hpk-1 failed to significantly increase autophagosomes (Figure 8J)
evidence: This is supported by autophagy reporter assay data with RNAi shown in Figure 8J.

claim: HPK-1-mediated induction of autophagy requires mxl-2, hlh-30, and daf-16.
source: thus HPK-1-mediated induction of autophagy requires mxl-2, hlh-30, and daf-16.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments.

claim: hlh-30 is required for the induction of autophagosomes in seam cells when hpk-1 is overexpressed in GABAergic neurons.
source: To rigorously test whether hpk-1 overexpression required hlh-30 for the induction of autophagosomes, we crossed the hlh-30 null mutation into animals overexpressing hpk-1 within GABAergic neurons (unc-47p::hpk-1;hlh-30(tm1978);lgg-1p::GFP::LGG-1); we find that hlh-30 is required for the induction of autophagosomes in seam cells when hpk-1 is overexpressed in GABAergic neurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by autophagy reporter assay data in hlh-30 mutants shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inactivation of either daf-15 (Raptor) or let-363 (TOR) increased lifespan and required mxl-2.
source: Indeed, we find that inactivation of either daf-15 (Raptor) or let-363 (TOR) increased lifespan and required mxl-2, as mxl-2(tm1516) null mutant animals failed to increase lifespan in the absence of TORC1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: MXL-2 functions as a heterodimer with MML-1.
source: MXL-2 functions as a heterodimer with MML-1 (Pickett et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: One of the human homologs of MML-1, carbohydrate response element binding protein (ChREBP/MondoB/MLXIPL/WBSCR14), maps within a deleted region in Williams-Beuren syndrome patients, which among other symptoms causes metabolic dysfunction, silent diabetes, and premature aging.
source: Interestingly, one of the human homologs of MML-1, carbohydrate response element binding protein (ChREBP/MondoB/MLXIPL/WBSCR14), maps within a deleted region in Williams-Beuren syndrome patients, which among other symptoms causes metabolic dysfunction, silent diabetes, and premature aging (Pober, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: HPK-1 regulates serotonergic signals to improve survival in acute thermal stress, likely through HSF-1.
source: Collectively, we conclude that HPK-1 regulates serotonergic signals to improve survival in acute thermal stress, likely through HSF-1, and initiates GABAergic signals to extend longevity through increased autophagy, which is linked to decreased TORC1 signaling and regulation of the Myc TFs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell-type specific experiments and represents an inference about mechanism.

claim: HPK-1 initiates GABAergic signals to extend longevity through increased autophagy, which is linked to decreased TORC1 signaling and regulation of the Myc TFs.
source: Collectively, we conclude that HPK-1 regulates serotonergic signals to improve survival in acute thermal stress, likely through HSF-1, and initiates GABAergic signals to extend longevity through increased autophagy, which is linked to decreased TORC1 signaling and regulation of the Myc TFs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell-type specific experiments and genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: During aging in wild-type animals, increasing damage and dysfunction is mitigated by the activation of stress response programs.
source: This comprehensive empirical dataset provides foundational support for a key theme in aging research: during aging in wild-type animals, increasing damage and dysfunction is mitigated by the activation of stress response programs.
evidence: This is a statement of a key concept in aging research, supported by the C. elegans Aging Atlas dataset.

claim: Human HIPK2 is activated in frontal cortex samples of patients with AD, in motor neurons of ALS patients, and in mouse models of ALS.
source: Consistently, the presence of human neurodegenerative disorders, a severe form of neuronal proteotoxic stress, correlates with activation of human hpk-1 expression: for example, human HIPK2 is activated in frontal cortex samples of patients with AD, in motor neurons of ALS patients, and in mouse models of ALS (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Overexpression of hpk-1 in the C. elegans nervous system may extend longevity by preemptively delaying the accumulation of age-associated damage and dysfunction to the proteome.
source: Thus, our results suggest that overexpression of hpk-1 in the C. elegans nervous system may extend longevity by preemptively delaying the accumulation of age-associated damage and dysfunction to the proteome (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: hpk-1 homologs in more complex metazoans can also promote cell death, a key homeostatic component of tissue regeneration.
source: However, hpk-1 homologs in more complex metazoans can also promote cell death, a key homeostatic component of tissue regeneration, indicating that chronic activation of HIPKs is not always beneficial (Calzado et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: hpk-1 prevents age-associated decline of axonal and synaptic integrity, which together preserve neuronal function during the aging process and thus also promote longer healthspan.
source: We find that hpk-1 prevents age-associated decline of axonal and synaptic integrity, which together preserve neuronal function during the aging process and thus also promote longer healthspan.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurodegeneration and synaptic function assays.

claim: Adult hipk2-/- mice display normal neurogenesis but manifest delayed-onset severe psychomotor and behavioral deficiencies, as well as degeneration of dopaminergic neurons, reminiscent of PD.
source: In support of this concept, adult hipk2-/- mice display normal neurogenesis but manifest delayed-onset severe psychomotor and behavioral deficiencies, as well as degeneration of dopaminergic neurons, reminiscent of PD (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Increased neuropeptide signaling has been associated with extended C. elegans longevity and is considered protective in AD.
source: For example, one-third of all neuropeptides are induced in the absence of hpk-1; yet increased neuropeptide signaling has been associated with extended C. elegans longevity and is considered protective in AD (Chen et al., 2018; Hodge et al., 2022; Petrella et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Loss of egl-3, a neuropeptide processing gene, extends longevity by inactivating processing of insulins.
source: For example, loss of egl-3, a neuropeptide processing gene, extends longevity by inactivating processing of insulins (Hamilton et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: egl-3 is upregulated in hpk-1 loss of function.
source: and egl-3 is upregulated in hpk-1 loss of function.
evidence: This is based on the RNA-seq data.

claim: Mutations within sensory neurons can alter longevity.
source: For example, loss of hpk-1 induces expression of intraflagellar transport (IFT) components in sensory cilia. Mutations within sensory neurons can alter longevity (Alcedo and Kenyon, 2004; Apfeld and Kenyon, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Decreased IFT during C. elegans aging impairs sensory perception and metabolism.
source: and decreased IFT during C. elegans aging impairs sensory perception and metabolism (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Deficiencies in primary cilia impairs neurogenesis in AD transgenic mice, resulting in accumulation of Aβ42 and tau protein and disease progression.
source: Deficiencies in primary cilia impairs neurogenesis in AD transgenic mice, resulting in accumulation of Aβ42 and tau protein and disease progression (Armato et al., 2013; Chakravarthy et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2022; Morelli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: HPK-1 expression in serotonergic neurons activates a cell non-autonomous signal to prime induction of molecular chaperones in muscle cells.
source: We show that HPK-1 expression in serotonergic neurons activates a cell non-autonomous signal to prime induction of molecular chaperones in muscle cells, whereas HPK-1 expression in GABAergic neurons signals induces autophagy in hypodermal tissue (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: HPK-1 expression in GABAergic neurons signals induces autophagy in hypodermal tissue.
